community-s8f/u1.input: A big part of why I think community matters for kids is Jean Liedloff's The Continuum Concept. Keep in mind that it's one outsider's interpretation of the Ye'kuana, and she may be idealizing what she saw. Still, it's a powerful picture. In her account, they carry their babies with them and bring them into daily adult life. Children are around people of several ages and learn by taking part, and a single exhausted parent isn't expected to be a child's whole social world. While a nuclear household can imitate some of this, a real village can make it normal.
community-s8f/u1.A: Community is a big reason why I think it's important for kids. Check out some of the ways the Yekuana raise their children (see also the Continuum Concept by Jean Liedloff, but remember that this is her interpretation of the Yekuana, and it's from the point of view of an outsider who might be romanticizing their culture.) They carry their babies with them, include them in their daily activities, expose their children to people of a few different ages, and let the children learn by participating. Also, parents aren't expected to be their kids' entire social world, and they're not expected to be able to do it all without being totally exhausted. While some of these things can be done to some extent in a nuclear family setting, I think it's really helpful to have a village that does these things.
community-s8f/u1.B: One of the reasons I think a community is a good thing for children is covered in the book The Continuum Concept by Jean Liedloff. It is definitely an outsiders view on the Ye'kuana people and she does seem to glorify some of what she saw, but I think that the idea of carrying the babies and including them in the daily life of adults, making sure they have contact with several different age groups of people, and allowing them to learn through participation, while still holding the parents to not being expected to do everything for a child social development wise when they are tired out from just taking care of them physically, is something that can't really be faked in a nuclear family living setup, but could easily be incorporated in a village type setup.

The review from the kids, once they're grown, matters more than founders usually want it to. Adults can talk forever about what they intended. The kids who lived through it might have something else to say.

community-s8f/u3.input:
Experiments where kids don't sleep and live with their parents need special caution. Research on Israeli kibbutzim found that they ended the practice of kids sleeping communally for a mix of reasons: developmental findings, parents' preferences and social change. Kids can benefit from high-quality group care and many loving adults in their lives, but replacing a secure attachment to their parents is a different matter.

People should look directly at what's going on at Tamera's Children's Place instead of caricaturing it. Still, my biased opinion is that I prefer a system where kids are exposed to more people, but where their bond with their parents isn't made ideologically inconvenient.
community-s8f/u3.A:
When making experiments like this one, where kids are not sleeping with their parents, one really has to be careful to do it right. The Israeli kibbutzim stopped the idea of kids sleeping together after doing experiments and found, amongst other reasons, that it was not good for the development of the kids, and that the parents did not want it, and it was not in accordance with social changes. Kids profit a lot of being taken care of in groups of people, if the quality is good, and they profit of having many loving people around them, but this doesn't replace being attached to the parents.

I invite anyone who is interested to not caricature, but to look at what's being done at the Children's Place in Tamera. Even though I am biased, I think that it is much better to have kids in contact with more people, without making it inconvenient for them to still be attached to their parents, which is made so by the ideology there.
community-s8f/u3.B:
That was exactly the kind of experiment that needs the greatest possible caution. Israeli Kibbutzim stopped the communal sleeping of their children for a variety of reasons, not the least of them being scientific findings on child development, but also parental wishes and social developments. The scientific consensus is that while children can benefit from high quality group care and many loving adults around, this does not replace secure attachment to their parents.

In any case, I'd suggest that instead of caricaturing what's going on in Tamera's Children's Place, to take a look at it first. And being honest, my biased view is that I prefer the system in which children get to interact with more people, instead of having to find it ideologically inconvenient for bonding to their parents.

community-s8f/u4.input:
This could come out wrong, so the safeguards need to be spelled out. A children's territory can't be left unmonitored by adults, or become a place where older kids quietly lord it over younger ones, or where secrecy gets treated as independence.

And I think it's a real problem that so many suburban folks treat any warm relationship between a kid and an adult who isn't related to them as suspicious. It's good for kids to have a whole bunch of grownups who know them and enjoy them, who notice when something changes, and who will act when something is wrong. That kind of fear can destroy the gift without actually preventing abuse.
community-s8f/u4.A:
To be clear - I'm saying this could be done in a way that would be inappropriate. There would need to be safeguards in place, because I'd certainly not want a territory for kids where there were no adults or where older kids ruled over the younger kids or where secrecy was encouraged.

On the other hand, I think there's a problem in many suburbs today of fearing any close relationships between kids and non-related adults. It would be good for kids to have lots of adults who enjoy them and who are watching out for them and who are willing to step in when needed.
community-s8f/u4.B:
This needs to be said carefully because it could be misconstrued. I don't mean to say that there shouldn't be adults around, or that older kids should be allowed to run younger kids around, or that secrets should be allowed.

I think that one of the problems of suburbs is the fear that many people have of allowing kids to have any kind of relationship with adults who are not related to them. Kids need lots of adults who like them. This fear is killing that.

community-s8f/u5.input:
The protection has several parts:

Give children real agency. They have the right to say "no," and no grownup has a right to a child's affection, physical contact, obedience outside of legitimate safety needs, or private access to them.

Have a no-secrets rule. No grownup may ever make a child keep a secret from their mom or another adult the child trusts, whether it's a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation or a relationship. Even surprises have to have an ending date when they're told. Secrets meant to isolate the child are forbidden.
community-s8f/u5.A:
There are several parts to this protection.

One is teaching the child that he can say "no" and that no grownup has a right to his affection, his physical contact, his obedience (not related to legitimate protection needs), or to him in private.

The second is teaching the child that no grownup has the right to ask him to keep secrets from his mom or another trusted adult. No grownup has the right to ask him to keep from his mom gifts, games, touching, conversations, or relationships. Yes, surprises have to eventually be told, so there needs to be an ending date attached to them, but no grownup has the right to ask a child to keep secrets that tend to cut him off from his mom or another trusted adult.
community-s8f/u5.B:
These are all important parts of how to protect yourself:

Remember that kids have a right to say no. No grownup has a right to a kid’s love, physical contact (unless it’s for legitimate safety reasons), obedience, or presence in their life.

Never keep secrets. No grownup has the right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or someone they trust. This applies to things, games, touch, conversations, relationships, etc. Surprise is different because at the end of a certain date, the surprise has to be told. Never keep secrets to isolate the kid.

community-s8f/u6.input:
Teach truthfulness before there's a crisis. Kids should know that their words have power, and that adults will listen to what they say and take it seriously. Don't interrogate them, or punish them if they aren't sure of everything, and don't let the teaching become a reason to dismiss what they report. A scared or confused kid may not tell the story perfectly and still need protecting.

Hear the child even when they point a finger at someone people love. Communities fail here, because the adult may be charismatic, useful, rich, spiritually important, or everybody's friend. Be clear about the process ahead of time, before anyone's face is attached to it. Do whatever's needed right away to keep everyone safe, then make sure it's investigated competently and fairly, and that nobody's status buys silence.
community-s8f/u6.A:
This is something that all of the kids need to be taught, even before there's a problem. Teach them that what they say is important. Teach them that what they say will be heard, that they won't be interrogated or punished for not knowing exactly what happened, or for not remembering it perfectly. Teach them that what they say won't be dismissed.

And as a community, all of the adults need to be willing to listen to what the kids have to say - even if it implicates someone that they love. All too often, when kids say something, the adults get defensive on behalf of the accused - because he's such a nice guy, or because he's doing so much for the community, or because he's rich and famous, or because he's got some other lever of power that they're afraid to offend, or because he's a really important spiritual leader, or because he's their good buddy. So explain to them the process that will be followed when they come to tell of problems - and then make sure that process is followed. Do whatever needs to be done immediately to secure the safety of everyone involved, and then make sure the matter is investigated in a competent and fair manner.
community-s8f/u6.B:
First, take the time to teach kids the importance of telling the truth, and that they will be heard, not interrogated or punished for their uncertainty, or belittled for their lack of ability to present the truth perfectly.

Second, when a kid says that someone they love has done this, listen to the kid, even though it is difficult. Too often in these situations the communities are not strong enough to acknowledge a kid’s testimony because the accused is too charismatic, or too useful, or too rich, or too important spiritually, or too connected with the people. Make sure that everyone knows how these situations will be dealt with, and then have the courage to do what is right for everyone immediately and to have it dealt with competently and fairly.

community-s8f/u7.input: Make sure kids have relationships and a reporting route outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give them perspective on their life, and someone to talk to. Make sure there's at least one trusted adult, advocate or reporting route they can reach without going through the community's leadership. In 1984, Vermont authorities seized 112 children in the Island Pond raid, but a court sent them back after rejecting the state's blanket request. So state intervention can fail spectacularly, and closing a community off completely can fail too. Kids need more than one world.
community-s8f/u7.A: One thing to make sure is that the kids still have connections to people outside of the community, like grandparents or cousins or local friends or teachers. This will give them a perspective of how their lives relate to the outside world. Also make sure the kids have at least one trusted adult they can talk to, advocate for them and provide a way for them to report problems outside of the community leadership. In 1984, 112 kids were seized by the state of Vermont during the Island Pond raid, but when the state tried to hold them the court sent them back because the state didn't go through the trouble to prove each case individually. So don't count on the state to step in. And don't count on being able to close the community off completely either.
community-s8f/u7.B: Well, there's some provisions one could imagine that might make this palatable. For one, make sure that the kids have lots of good relationships on the outside. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers, whatever. It'll help give the kids context for what they're experiencing in their life, and make sure there's someone they can talk to. Ideally, at least one trusted adult, advocate, or reporting route that doesn't run through the community leadership. This is important because in 1984, during the Island Pond raid , the state seized 112 children, only to have a court send them right back because they didn't like the blanket request. So it's possible to completely fail at shutting a community down, and if they're completely closed off...

community-s8f/u8.input: I also searched the research corpus for a single well-documented case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to other people, with a good record of the whole sequence: what they did, how it was assessed, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. I failed to find one. It may be that cases came up but were handled in private, or sent somewhere else, but it means I can't claim communities already know how to handle the hardest version on their own. The child, the family, and anyone at risk all need access to competent help and review, outside the control of the home community.
community-s8f/u8.A: I have looked through a lot of relevant research, which has been accumulated during my research into various issues relating to intentional communities, and I am unable to find an example of any child who grew up in such a community who remained seriously dangerous to people, where the behaviour and the handling of the case was well documented. This doesn't mean that there aren't such cases, but, to my mind, it at least suggests that the case should be handled outside the community, and that the child, their family, and the community should have access to people who are competent in dealing with this kind of situation, and a review process.
community-s8f/u8.B: This is an important point, and it occurred to me to look for a single well-documented case where an intentional community tried this approach and it failed , i.e., the child still turned out to be seriously dangerous to other people, and there's a good record of the whole sequence, the 'what they did', the assessment, the intervention, the review, and the later outcome. Surprisingly I failed to find a single such case in the entire research corpus that I've gathered. That probably doesn't mean that there aren't any, but it does suggest that the communities need to have access to competent help that is not within their control, both for the child and the family.

community-s8f/u9.input:
The Amish let their young people decide on their own whether to join the church once they're adults, and roughly 85 percent or more eventually do. Popular culture tends to blow Rumspringa out of proportion, as if every teenager went wild, but adult baptism still matters, because it makes belonging a commitment instead of a fact imposed at birth.

If the children never leave, the community can't know whether they'd come back freely. So let them study, travel, make friends, see other ways of life, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors.
community-s8f/u9.A:
It is important to remember that the vast majority (85% or more) of Amish youth do choose to join the church when they become adults, and that the Rumspringa is largely blown out of proportion by popular culture. It is still important, however, for the Amish to not be baptized until they are adults.

If the kids never leave, there's no way to tell if they would come back, even if they want to. Allow them the freedom to go out and learn what they want to learn, see what they want to see and disagree with the thoughts of the founders.
community-s8f/u9.B:
It's not quite true that the Amish "allow their children to leave". It's true that they allow their children to choose whether to join the church upon reaching adulthood. About 85% or more of Amish do choose to join the church. Pop culture's portrayal of the Rumspringa is grossly exaggerated. The point is, though, that they are baptized as adults.

If they aren't allowed to leave how will they ever know if they want to come back? Let them explore the world, let them learn, let them travel, let them socialise, let them see if they believe the teachings of their founders or not.

community-s8f/u10.input: Every childhood narrows the future. Most ordinary parents aren't going to give their kid a bunch of money at 18 and say, "Go see the world." They'll try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer, and food, medical care and basic survival may rightly come first.
community-s8f/u10.A: It depends on how the person was raised. Most normal parents aren't gonna give their kid a pile of money at 18 and tell them to go see the world. They'll work on getting their child ready for the next step. And if their from a poor or no money community, they probably won't have the money to do this, so all they can do is try to keep their kid fed, healthy and alive.
community-s8f/u10.B: It depends on what they did in their childhood as that will shape what they can do in the future. Also its not like most people will just give their kid a bunch of money at 18 and tell them to go see the world. They will likely be trying to prepare them for a next step that will actually work. And if they are coming from a community that is poor or has no money then they likely will be focused on getting food and medical care and just surviving.

community-s8f/u11.input: The realistic standard isn't unlimited freedom. It's that leaving shouldn't be made artificially impossible. Kids who grow up without using money especially need to know enough about how the money world works that they aren't helpless in it: jobs, rent, contracts, banking, scams, ID, getting around, and how to ask for help. They need skills and an education they can take with them, relationships outside the community, access to their records and documents, and at least one plausible next step, whether that's school, an apprenticeship, work, family or another community. If the community can help out with temporary housing, travel, tools, or a small reserve for the transition, great. But even if it can't, it can at least avoid punishing people for leaving, or withholding the knowledge and records a young adult needs to function somewhere else. No upbringing gives perfect freedom. The point isn't to erase path dependence. It's to not turn belonging into a trap.
community-s8f/u11.A: That’s the realistic standard, not some hand-wavy “they can do whatever they want because they’re free!” If someone grew up with no experience in the money-world, they certainly need to be educated in how that works. But beyond that, it’s pretty easy to imagine a community in which people who want to leave are helped to develop some transferable skills/education, some relationships with people outside the community, access to their records and documents, and some options for where they might go (school, apprenticeship, work, family, some other community…) as well as some material help with the transition. If the community doesn’t have the resources to do that, it can at least avoid punishing people for leaving and making sure they have the knowledge and records they need. Nothing gives people complete freedom from path-dependence, but it’s not that hard to avoid trapping people.
community-s8f/u11.B: For a reasonable realistic standard for allowing people to leave, how about not making it artificially impossible? Specifically, for kids who have never dealt with money, teaching them about the money world so they know how to deal with it if necessary. More generally, leaving kids with skills and education that make it possible for them to succeed in the outside world if they so choose, not being actively hostile to them making social connections outside the community, making sure they have access to their records and documents, and giving them at least one obvious next option to go to (school, apprenticeship, job, family, another community, etc.). It’s also helpful if the community has enough resources to help people leave (by providing temporary housing or transportation or tools or whatever), but if it doesn’t, there are still a lot of things it can do to help. And if it doesn’t have those, there are still a lot of things it can not do that would make leaving harder. No way of raising kids gives them complete freedom, but it’s possible to not be too path dependent.

community-s8f/u12.input:
Some may leave for good, and others may start their own communities with different values instead of waiting decades to inherit the original one. Parents may feel that as a loss, even when it's the movement evolving.

Couples who share a home, a culture and a bed still split over screens, vaccines, schooling, religion, food, discipline and medical care. Now multiply that by twenty adults with twenty different childhoods.

Goodwill doesn't answer those questions once there are children in the middle of the disagreement. Communities need enough shared principles about raising children to offer coherence, and enough room for parents to still be parents.
community-s8f/u12.A:
How many will permanently leave, or start their own communities to live according to their values, instead of waiting 20 or 30 years to inherit the community they're in now (which, at least from the parents' point of view, sounds like a loss to the community)?

Couples that live together, share the same culture, and even share a bed, often split up over disagreements about computer screens, vaccinations, schooling, religion, food, child discipline, medical care, etc. - how can 20 people with 20 different childhoods avoid it?

What do do when "good will" is not enough - especially when children are involved? How much common ground on principles is needed to have a coherent community while still leaving enough room for each parent to parent?
community-s8f/u12.B:
Well, yeah, some will break off. It's also possible some will found their own communities with their values rather than expect to inherit the community in like 30 or so years. The parents will probably feel like that's a loss.

Lots of couples sharing a home, a culture and a bed break up over different ideas about screens, vaccinating, schooling, religion, food, how to punish kids, how to treat kids when they're ill, etc. Multiply that by twenty adults with twenty different experiences of how they were brought up.

When kids get involved it's hard to smooth over with goodwill. It's going to have to be a mix of sufficient shared principles and sufficient flexibility to let the parents be parents.
